title: Support vectors & the margin
intro: The secret of SVMs: most of your training data can be removed without changing the model. The examples that do matter are called support vectors.
keyPoints: An SVM looks for the boundary with the largest margin between the classes.
Only the support vectors (closest to the boundary) drive the fit — the other points can go.
Hinge loss + L2 penalty = exactly the max-margin solution.
The margin is the distance from the boundary to the nearest points; larger = more breathing room.

blocks.html: A linear SVM = linear classifier with hinge loss + standard L2 regularization. The crucial difference with logistic loss: the flat part — once the raw output exceeds +1 the loss is exactly zero and the example contributes nothing to the fit.

blocks.label: SVM = hinge + L2
blocks.caption: The standard SVM: hinge loss per example plus L2 regularisation on the coefficients.

sections.title: Support vectors: the examples that matter

blocks.html: Support vectors are the examples with \( y_i f(x_i) \le 1 \): misclassified or correct but close to the boundary. The rest can be discarded without effect — kernel-SVMs therefore scale with the number of support vectors, not with n.

blocks.caption: How much of your data is actually a support vector?
blocks.source:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)

svc = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1.0).fit(X, y)

print('Training examples  :', len(X))
print('Support vectors    :', len(svc.support_vectors_))
print('Per class          :', svc.n_support_)
print('Training score     :', round(svc.score(X, y), 3))

blocks.html: Remove a non-support vector → the model does not change. Remove a support vector → the model does change. Support vectors are literally the examples that "carry" the model.

The max-margin view: on linearly separable data the learned boundary sits exactly halfway between both classes and the SVM maximizes the margin. This is mathematically equivalent to hinge loss + L2 — two lenses, same model.

blocks.label: margin
blocks.caption: The width of the buffer zone around the decision boundary. Maximising the margin = minimising ‖w‖ — hence the L2 penalty.

blocks.html: Why does this work exactly? The hinge loss demands correct predictions with a margin (\( y\,f(x) \ge 1 \)); the L2 term keeps \( \lVert w \rVert \) small — and together that pushes the boundary exactly into the middle.
